entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3510"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 16</title> <div sID="gen4963" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.1-2Kgs.16.16">2Ki 16:1-16</reference>. Ahaz' Wicked Reign over Judah.<div eID="gen4963" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4964" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3510"/><hi type="bold">1-4. Ahaz ... did not that which was right in the sight of the Lord--</hi>[See on <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.1">2Ch 28:1</reference>.] The character of this king's reign, the voluptuousness and religious degeneracy of all classes of the people, are graphically portrayed in the writings of Isaiah, who prophesied at that period. The great increase of worldly wealth and luxury in the reigns of Azariah and Jotham had introduced a host of corruptions, which, during his reign, and by the influence of Ahaz, bore fruit in the idolatrous practices of every kind which prevailed in all parts of the kingdom (see <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.24">2Ch 28:24</reference>). <div eID="gen4964" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3514"/><div sID="gen4970" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3514"/><hi type="bold">7-9. So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser--</hi>In spite of the assurance given him by Isaiah by two signs, the one immediate, the other remote (<reference osisRef="Isa.7.14">Is 7:14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.8.4">8:4</reference>), that the confederate kings would not prevail against him, Ahaz sought aid from the Assyrian monarch, to purchase which he sent the treasures of the palace and temple. Tiglath-pileser marched against Damascus, slew Rezin the king, and carried the people of Damascus into captivity to Kir, which is thought to have been the city Karine (now Kerend), in Media. <div eID="gen4970" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 7-9. So Ahaz sent messengers to Tiglath-pileser-- In spite of the assurance given him by Isaiah by two signs, the one immediate, the other remote ( Is 7:14 ; 8:4 ), that the confederate kings would not prevail against him, Ahaz sought aid from the Assyrian monarch, to purchase which he sent the treasures of the palace and temple. Tiglath-pileser marched against Damascus, slew Rezin the king, and carried the people of Damascus into captivity to Kir, which is thought to have been the city Karine (now Kerend), in Media.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3515"/><div sID="gen4971" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3515"/><hi type="bold">10-16. And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser--</hi>This was a visit of respect, and perhaps of gratitude. During his stay in that heathen city, Ahaz saw an altar with which he was greatly captivated. Forthwith a sketch of it was transmitted to Jerusalem, with orders to Urijah the priest to get one constructed according to the Damascus model, and let this new altar supersede the old one in the temple. Urijah, with culpable complaisance, acted according to his instructions (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.16">2Ki 16:16</reference>). The sin in this affair consisted in meddling with, and improving according to human taste and fancy, the altars of the temple, the patterns of which had been furnished by divine authority (<reference osisRef="Exod.25.40">Ex 25:40</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.26.30">26:30</reference>; <reference osisRef="Exod.27.1">27:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Chr.28.19">1Ch 28:19</reference>). Urijah was one of the witnesses taken by Isaiah to bear his prediction against Syria and Israel (<reference osisRef="Isa.8.2">Is 8:2</reference>).<div eID="gen4971" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen4972" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.16.17-2Kgs.16.19">2Ki 16:17-19</reference>. He Spoils the Temple. <div eID="gen4972" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 10-16. And king Ahaz went to Damascus to meet Tiglath-pileser-- This was a visit of respect, and perhaps of gratitude. During his stay in that heathen city, Ahaz saw an altar with which he was greatly captivated. Forthwith a sketch of it was transmitted to Jerusalem, with orders to Urijah the priest to get one constructed according to the Damascus model, and let this new altar supersede the old one in the temple. Urijah, with culpable complaisance, acted according to his instructions ( 2Ki 16:16 ). The sin in this affair consisted in meddling with, and improving according to human taste and fancy, the altars of the temple, the patterns of which had been furnished by divine authority ( Ex 25:40 ; 26:30 ; 27:1 ; 1Ch 28:19 ). Urijah was one of the witnesses taken by Isaiah to bear his prediction against Syria and Israel ( Is 8:2 ). 2Ki 16:17-19 . He Spoils the Temple.

The change made by Ahaz consisted in removing both of these into the temple from fear of the king of Assyria, that, in case of a siege, he might secure the entrance of the temple from him. <chapter eID="2Kgs.16"/>
entries.content_plain: 18. the covert for the Sabbath-- the portico through which the priests entered the temple on the Sabbath. the king's entry without-- a private external entrance for the king into the temple. The change made by Ahaz consisted in removing both of these into the temple from fear of the king of Assyria, that, in case of a siege, he might secure the entrance of the temple from him.
